extracted.subtask_description: Close exposition of how the mind forms ideas of number, space, and duration and the proper way to conceive 'infinity'; includes conditions for correct numbering and conceptual distinctions to avoid confusion about the infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of names for numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Names or marks for each distinct combination of units are more necessary in numbers than in other ideas; without such names or marks we can hardly make use of numbers in reckoning, especially for large combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: some Americans could not count to 1000 because their language had no words for larger numbers; the Tououpinambos had names only up to 5 and used fingers beyond that. Distinct denominations (e.g., giving every six figures a new name) conduce to clear numeration; lacking them leads to confusion and the notion of a mere heap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for correct numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: To reckon right it is required: (1) that the mind distinguish carefully two ideas different only by the addition or subtraction of ONE unit; (2) that it retain in memory the names or marks of the several combinations from one unit up to the target number, and in the exact order the numbers follow one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If either requirement fails, the chain breaks and progress in numbering halts; one retains only a confused idea of multitude rather than distinct numeration. This explains why some children or persons never learn to count beyond moderate series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number as the measure of all measurables
rubrics_metrics.description: Number is what the mind uses in measuring all things that are measurable, principally expansion (space) and duration (time); our idea of infinity, even when applied to space and duration, is essentially the infinity of number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When conceiving immensity or eternity the mind uses repeated additions of known measures (miles, years, millions) — thus number underlies and structures our ideas of other magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of infinity derived from repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind forms the idea of infinity by observing its power to repeat any given idea (a foot, a day, a number) and to add it without end; this ENDLESS ADDITION or ADDIBILITY furnishes the clearest idea of infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish forming the idea (mental endless progression) from asserting actual existence of an infinite thing; the former arises from mental repetition and is how we come by the notion of infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinity applies only to ideas having parts (quantities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only ideas that are considered as having parts and capable of increase by addition (space, duration, number) afford an idea of infinity; ideas that do not consist of parts (e.g., whiteness, sweetness) cannot be augmented into infinity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: adding another 'white' perception does not increase the idea of whiteness as parts do; thus speaking of infinite sweetness or infinite whiteness is a category mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish 'infinity of X' from 'X infinite'
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully distinguish between the idea of the infinity of space (an endless progression in thought) and the idea of a space infinite (an actually infinite, fully comprehended space); the former is a growing idea, the latter is a contradictory attempt to have a completed infinite idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joining infinity to a terminated, positive idea (i.e., treating a bounded idea as already infinite) leads to confusion; one must treat infinity as an uncompleted, endless process rather than a completed magnitude the mind fully contains.

rubrics_metrics.name: No positive/comprehensive idea of the actual infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: We have no positive, clear idea of an actually infinite number, space, or duration; the idea of infinity consists primarily in the negation of an end (the power of further addition) rather than a positive, determinate conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A test: ask whether one could add to the supposed infinite; if addition remains possible, the idea is not genuinely comprehensive. Claims of possessing a positive idea of infinity are mistaken and generate paradoxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of number to conceive immensity and eternity
rubrics_metrics.description: When conceiving infinite space or duration the mind practically uses numbers (millions of miles or years) as the distinct ideas by which it approximates an idea of infinity; number affords the clearest route to the notion of endlessness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mental strategy: aggregate many known finite measures (millions, millions, etc.) to approach the idea of inexhaustible addibility; nevertheless the residual 'beyond' remains obscure and negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinite divisibility is another form of infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind can also conceive infinity by dividing units into ever smaller fractions (infinite divisibility); this is analogous to endless addition and likewise does not yield a positive idea of an actually infinitely small thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infinite divisibility is effectively the same infinite process as repeated addition, and any attempt to form a completed positive idea of infinitesimal size encounters the same obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eternity implies succession; avoid punctum stans
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of eternal duration, insofar as we apprehend it, involves an infinite succession of moments of duration; one cannot coherently conceive duration without succession, so 'duration without succession' (punctum stans) is unintelligible here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therefore, conceptions of eternity that attempt to remove succession fail to give a clearer, positive idea of infinite duration; treat eternity as endless succession rather than as a static, completed state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of human ideas about infinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties and paradoxes in discourse about infinity mark a defect in our ideas; we ought not to assume we possess clear, complete conceptions of infinity but acknowledge that much of what lies beyond our positive ideas is obscure and negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical caution: avoid asserting detailed positive features of infinite things; accept that our conception of 'so much greater' beyond any finite idea is indeterminate and cannot be comprehensively represented.
